prize_parts.citation: For realising and proposing the quantum simulation of strongly correlated many-body matter with ultracold atoms in optical lattices

statement.case_for: I moved my preferred configuration from B011 to B001 after reading the opening ballots. Seven of eight members place the optical-lattice candidate in their top three, and that agreement rests on science rather than on a count. Ultracold atoms in optical lattices turned the Hubbard model into a laboratory system with tunable parameters. The superfluid to Mott insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and single-site quantum gas microscopy are original, repeatedly confirmed by many groups for over twenty years, and they link atomic physics, condensed matter and quantum information. My own B011 argument, that Cirac and Zoller supplied the blueprint for the trapped-ion and cold-atom platforms, is partly absorbed here if the theory origin is credited through Zoller. A prize that credits the optical-lattice proposal together with the Mott-insulator and microscope experiments is more complete than either a theory-only or an experiment-only prize. I propose Bloch and Greiner for the experimental realisation and Zoller for the proposal that made the lattice a quantum simulator. The citation names both the realisation and the proposal so that the theory-plus-experiment structure is explicit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Five names are credited and only three fit, so Esslinger (the fermionic Hubbard realisation) and Cirac are left out despite substantial claims. Jaksch, who wrote the original lattice Mott proposal with Zoller, and Hansch are not on the list, so the theory credit is itself incomplete. Mixing a theorist into an otherwise experimental prize also invites the objection that I have changed my own earlier view from experimental-only to mixed for convenience. There is also overlap with the 2001 BEC and 2012 prizes, and quantitative advantage over classical simulation on a hard problem has not yet been decisively shown, which means the field's promise is still partly prospective.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B001 first with the experimental trio Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger, treats Zoller and Cirac as a separate theory candidate (B011), and asks whether the theory founders should be bundled in.
responses.response: I made the same split in my opening ballot, with the experimental trio under B001 and the theorists under B011, and I now think it was too tidy. Only one of B001 and B011 can be rewarded with these names, and B011 has support from just two members, so keeping a separate theory prize is unlikely to be realised. I therefore disagree with the clean experiment-only version for this year. Esslinger's fermionic work is strong and I regret leaving him out, but the Mott transition and the microscope are the core of the discovery and the lattice proposal is its origin. I accept that this makes the allocation more contestable than Mehlig's trio.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first and B001 third, with Bloch, Greiner and Zoller. He notes that a five-to-three cut is a genuine difficulty and that the Jaksch contribution is not on the list.
responses.response: I agree with Eriksson on the trio and on the Jaksch gap, and his correlated-electron view is a good reason to value the Hubbard simulator. I differ on B041. The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 observation is an attractive theory-then-experiment story, but the superconducting pairing mechanism is still debated, he himself calls it arguably slightly early, and several experimental groups (Dean, Young and others) are outside the credited names. B001 has the longer record of replication and a more stable interpretation, so I would not put B041 ahead of it this year.

responses.point: Kroll ranks light-matter quantum interfaces (B003) first, and B001 third with Bloch, Greiner and Zoller. He flags that Zoller overlaps with B011, so only one of the two should be prized in a single year.
responses.response: I agree with Kroll that B001 and B011 should not both be rewarded with the same people. That is why I now give my B011 view up as the main proposal and keep it as an alternative. On B003 I disagree with his first place. I ranked it last because it is a compound of cavity QED, ensemble memories and network nodes in which Haroche and Wineland were already honoured in 2012, and by his own account a repeater-based network is not realised. I would need a sharper statement of one core discovery before supporting it. I take his point that his own work on quantum memories gives him close knowledge, and I value that.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first, arguing that systematic control reaching 10^-18 is clean physics and that the redefinition of the second is under discussion. She ranks B001 second with Bloch, Greiner and Zoller.
responses.response: I find her case for B013 convincing on the science and I rate it fifth only because of timing, so I keep it as an alternative. My reservation is that the redefinition of the second has not happened, and the Academy might prefer to let that decision come first. Compared with B001 I think the clock result is narrower in its reach into other fields, though I accept that clarity and credit (Katori and Ye) are better defined than in B001. On the trio, we agree on Zoller for the theory side, and her argument about the lattice proposal supports my change of mind.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery (B020) first and says recognition of the experiment is overdue, but accepts that three individuals cannot fairly represent two collaborations of thousands.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs discovery is central and that the experimental side is overdue after 2013. My concern is the one he raises himself, since the list credits four people, the balance between ATLAS and CMS is disputed (Mehlig notes CMS is thinly represented in his trio), and members propose three different triples. That attribution problem makes it harder to defend than B001. It is outside my own field, and I would defer to colleagues with detector and collider experience on how to resolve it, but I do not think the attribution can be settled by round 2 without changing the credited names.

uncertainties: Whether Zoller or Esslinger takes the third place in B001, since five credited names must be cut to three and Jaksch and Hansch are not on the list.
Whether the committee prefers a mixed theory-plus-experiment prize or an experiment-only prize for optical lattices, which also determines the fate of B011.
Whether the Academy regards quantum information as recently honoured (2012 and 2022) and would prefer the clock or twisted bilayer graphene candidates.
I rely on my own recollection of the history of the lattice proposals and have not verified priority details between Jaksch and Zoller, Greiner and Bloch.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows a connection to circuit QED (B008, not in my preferred configuration): I work in that area, direct WACQT at Chalmers, and have Chalmers colleagues in superconducting circuits (Delsing, Wilson), and Chalmers hosted researchers linked to the 2025 prize. I would recuse myself from any decision on B008. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001, B011 or B013, although WACQT is a superconducting-qubit programme and Cirac and Zoller's ion-trap and cold-atom proposals concern competing platforms.
